791.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Associate with the Holy people, who will take you to Nirvana in the end. Do not associate with the faithless cynics; they would bring you to ruin.”
791.explanation: Kabir's salok treats companionship as something that carries a person all the way to the end, for good or ill: the company of the holy stays with you to the last, while the company of the saakat (the faithless cynic) brings ruin.
791.tie_back: The Kural warns that a friendship, once made, cannot be shaken off, so choosing badly is the worst harm; Kabir likewise says the company you take up decides where you end, so it must be chosen before it binds you.
791.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 93 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
791._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on choosing companions with their final effect in view, but Kabir frames the choice spiritually (holy versus faithless) and does not state the Kural's specific point that loyal people cannot later drop a friend.

792.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have been ruined and destroyed by bad company, like the banana plant near the thorn bush. The thorn bush waves in the wind, and pierces the banana plant; see this, and do not associate with the faithless cynics.”
792.explanation: Kabir pictures a soft banana plant growing beside a thorny beri bush: every gust of wind drives the thorns into it, so the damage of bad company comes slowly, again and again, until it destroys.
792.tie_back: The Kural says friendship formed without repeated examination brings, in the end, grief that can kill; Kabir's banana plant is that slow, fatal wounding by a companion who was never tested.
792.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 88 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
792._accuracy_note: Close on the delayed, deadly harm of a bad companion; the Kural's stress on examining a person again and again before befriending is implied rather than stated.

793.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The mind has become a bird; it soars and flies in the ten directions. According to the company it keeps, so are the fruits it eats.”
793.explanation: Kabir says the restless mind settles wherever its company is, and what it becomes depends on that company, so the people around a person are a true index of what that person will become.
793.tie_back: The Kural tells us to check a would-be friend's character, faults and the circle he keeps close; Kabir explains why the circle matters, since a person takes the fruit of the company he keeps.
793.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 86 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
793._accuracy_note: Matches only the last item of the Kural's checklist (the circle one keeps); the Kural's test of family background (kudimai) has no Sikh counterpart, since Sikhism rejects judging people by birth.

794.quote_or_event: “The sight of them banishes my evil-mindedness; they are my only true friends. I have searched the whole world; O servant Nanak! How rare are such persons!”
794.explanation: Guru Arjan says the true friend is the one whose very presence drives out one's evil-mindedness, and such friends are so rare that he had to search the whole world for them.
794.tie_back: The Kural says the friendship of a person with a living sense of shame at wrongdoing is worth winning even at a price; Guru Arjan agrees that such a friend, who turns one away from wrong, is rare and worth any search.
794.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
794._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that a morally upright friend is rare and precious, but the Kural's first criterion, being born into a good family, conflicts with the Sikh rejection of caste and lineage, and Guru Arjan speaks of spiritual company rather than paying a price.

795.quote_or_event: When Guru Gobind Singh, passing through Narayana in Rajasthan, saluted the shrine of the saint Dadu by raising an arrow to his forehead, the Khalsa objected and one Sikh, Man Singh, quoted the Guru's own verse forbidding the worship of tombs. The Guru at once offered to pay a fine; after some debate the Sikhs fixed it at Rs 125, which they spent on a kitchen tent.
795.explanation: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism says the Guru did this to test the conviction of his Sikhs, and he welcomed being rebuked by them when he appeared to break his own teaching.
795.tie_back: The Kural tells us to seek friends who will rebuke us sharply and understand the world's ways; the Khalsa rebuking even its Guru, and the Guru accepting it, is the Sikh model of a fellowship that corrects rather than flatters.
795.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, ed. Harbans Singh (Punjabi University, Patiala), entry 'Dadu Dial (1544-1603)' by Gurnek Singh (paraphrase)
795._accuracy_note: A well-known episode that captures the value of followers who rebuke frankly, but it concerns a Guru and his Khalsa rather than two friends, and the encyclopedia's dating ('first decade of the seventeenth century') is evidently a slip for the early eighteenth century.

796.quote_or_event: “In good times, there are many companions around, but in bad times, there is no one at all. Says Nanak, vibrate, and meditate on the Lord; He shall be your only Help and Support in the end.”
796.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes that prosperity gathers companions and adversity scatters them, and he turns from fair-weather friends to God as the one support who remains.
796.tie_back: The Kural says even misfortune has one benefit, since it measures exactly how far friends will go for you; Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok records the result of that measurement: many in good times, none in bad.
796.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1428, Salok Mahalla 9 (salok 32), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
796._accuracy_note: Close on adversity revealing who one's companions really are; the Guru draws a devotional conclusion (rely on God) where the Kural draws a practical one (misfortune is a measuring rod).

797.quote_or_event: “Kabir! Do not associate with the faithless cynics; run far away from them. If you touch a vessel stained with soot, some of the soot will stick to you.”
797.explanation: Kabir uses the image of a soot-blackened pot: however careful you are, contact leaves a mark, so the only safe course with a bad companion is to get well away.
797.tie_back: The Kural says a person's real gain is to give up completely the friendship of fools; Kabir likewise counsels a clean break, since even slight contact with the wrong company leaves its stain.
797.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 131 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
797._accuracy_note: A strong match on wholly abandoning harmful company, though Kabir's saakat is the faithless worldling rather than the Kural's fool (pedhai), and the Kural frames leaving as profit rather than avoiding a stain.

798.quote_or_event: “The world is entangled in its own pleasures; no one is for anyone else. In good times, many come and sit together, surrounding you on all four sides. But when hard times come, they all leave, and no one comes near you.”
798.explanation: In this Sorath shabad Guru Tegh Bahadur describes companions who crowd around in comfort and vanish in distress, because their attachment was only to their own pleasure.
798.tie_back: The Kural forbids taking up the friendship of those who cut off their support in time of trouble; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes exactly those people, who leave as soon as hard times come.
798.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 634, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
798._accuracy_note: Matches the Kural's second line closely; its first line (not dwelling on thoughts that shrink the spirit) has no parallel here.

799.quote_or_event: “My teeth, feet, eyes and ears have stopped working. My body cries out, “Those whom I knew have left me!””
799.explanation: In this salok Sheikh Farid, whose verses are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, speaks in the voice of an old man near death whose body laments that the people close to him have gone.
799.tie_back: The Kural says the memory of friends who left you as you were falling burns the heart even at the hour of death; Farid's dying body likewise cries out over those who have left it.
799.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid 77 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
799._accuracy_note: Captures the anguish of being left by companions at life's end, but Farid's 'those whom I knew' (jaani) are more naturally loved ones who have died or gone than friends who betrayed him, so the Kural's specific sting of desertion is only partly present.

800.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I will remain in the Saadh Sangat, the Company of the Holy, even if I have only coarse bread to eat. Whatever will be, will be. I will not associate with the faithless cynics.”
800.explanation: Kabir resolves to hold to good company at any material cost, even a diet of coarse bread, and to refuse the company of faithless people whatever the consequences.
800.tie_back: The Kural says to cling to the friendship of the blameless and leave the unsuitable even if it costs you something; Kabir accepts poverty as the price of keeping good company and shunning bad.
800.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1369, Salok Bhagat Kabir 99 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
800._accuracy_note: A close parallel in both halves (cling to the good, shun the bad, at a price), though for Kabir the good company is the sangat of the holy rather than a personal friend.
